title: The Necessary Radiators
premise: Lior Dravenmoor, once the conservatory's most celebrated young pianist before a public breakdown ended her career, returns years later as a janitor, hiding in plain sight among the people who watched her fall. When she is assigned to clean the office of Mirela Ostrov, a dying linguist who is the last fluent speaker of Vessic—a language with no written form—Mirela asks her to become her final student. As Lior memorizes a language that exists only in two mouths and one fading memory, she is forced to confront why she stopped speaking musically, reconcile with her estranged former teacher Nadia, and finally give voice to everything she inventoried in silence. The novel ends with Mirela's death and Lior recording the last lesson, then performing publicly for the first time in nine years—playing not for applause but as an act of translation, keeping both the language and herself alive.
about_author: August Yarrow is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent eleven years listening to practice rooms through the walls before writing about them. Their essays on silence and institutional memory have appeared in small literary journals under three other names they no longer use.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. She works nights at the Halvard Conservatory, cataloguing the building's objects and her own unsaid sentences in a private notebook. A chance encounter with her former teacher Nadia in a stairwell nearly exposes her; Lior hides behind a mop cart. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of invisibility established.

chapters.title: The Office at the End of the Corridor
chapters.summary: Lior is assigned to clean Room 14B, where linguist Mirela Ostrov keeps boxes of reel-to-reel tapes. Mirela recognizes her from old recital programs and says so plainly, without pity. Lior flees, then returns. Emotional beat: being seen for the first time in years, and surviving it.

chapters.title: Vessic
chapters.summary: Mirela reveals she is the last speaker of Vessic and has months to live. She asks Lior—not a linguist, not a musician anymore—to be her final student. Lior refuses, citing her inventory of reasons. That night she plays one note on a discarded piano in the basement. Emotional beat: refusal that already sounds like yes.

chapters.title: Lessons Begin
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Lior and Mirela. Lessons happen during cleaning shifts: sounds first, meanings later. Mirela teaches by association, not grammar. Lior discovers Vessic has no word for 'prodigy' but eleven words for kinds of listening. Emotional beat: tentative joy, the first thing she has wanted in years.

chapters.title: What Nadia Kept
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. Flashbacks to Lior's breakdown at seventeen—the competition, the collapsed performance, the teacher who pushed too hard and said too little since. Nadia finds one of Lior's dropped notebook pages and understands what the janitor is carrying. Emotional beat: guilt meeting its mirror.

chapters.title: The Tapes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Digitizing Mirela's archive, Lior hears recordings of Mirela's mother and of students long dead, including a young singer whose voice stops mid-phrase. Mirela explains: some things end unfinished, and that is not failure. Lior begins speaking Vessic aloud, badly, in empty corridors. Emotional beat: permission to be imperfect.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: A university committee arrives to claim Mirela's materials for a proper archival project, dismissing Lior as 'the cleaning lady.' Mirela defends her choice of student; the committee threatens to move Mirela to a care facility. Lior almost retreats into invisibility, then signs her full name to the visitor log as Mirela's student. Emotional beat: choosing visibility despite institutional erasure.

chapters.title: The Word for Goodbye
chapters.summary: Mirela's POV, weakening. Hospital stays interrupt lessons. She teaches Lior the Vessic farewell ritual—a spoken blessing meant to be said by two people, each completing the other's sentence—and admits she never got to say it with her own mother. Emotional beat: grief arriving ahead of death, love made structural.

chapters.title: Two Mouths, One Memory
chapters.summary: Climax. Mirela's final lucid days. In the conservatory's empty recital hall, the two women perform the farewell ritual completely, each finishing the other's sentences in Vessic while Nadia secretly witnesses from the back row. Mirela dies three days later holding the recorder. Emotional beat: the goodbye said properly, out loud, in time.

chapters.title: Translation
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue-like. At Mirela's memorial, Lior takes the stage unannounced and performs—speaking Vessic between movements, translating the language into sound for an audience hearing it for the last first time. Nadia waits afterward, and they begin, haltingly, to talk. Lior closes her inventory notebook and starts a new one titled with a single Vessic word meaning 'beginning again.' Emotional beat: resurrection through voice.
